title: Signal Garden
description: A room of houseplants that play an ambient soundscape from their own electrical signals.

data.text: Plants are never still. Their leaves carry slow electrical changes all day, from light, water and touch. What if a room let you hear that?
Pothos in the café window turned toward the light in about a week. Something that slow should sound slow.
The music should be as ignorable as it is interesting.
data.cite: Brian Eno, liner notes for Music for Airports, 1978

items.text: Find out how big a plant's signal actually is
Ask the studio about a two-night open studio

items.content: Slow enough to notice you've slowed down.
Low light, warm speakers hidden in planters, nothing on the walls.

data.note: The album cover's greens and warm pinks. Soft, a bit funny, never clinical.
Capacitive sensing library. Touch on a leaf shows up cleanly.
Browser synth library. Lets the sound run on a laptop hidden in the room.

data.text: Two kinds of signal: a slow drift over minutes (light, watering) and quick spikes when someone touches a leaf. The drift sets the key and tempo; spikes trigger notes.
Most of what gets marketed as 'plant music' is a touch sensor with a nice synth on it. That's fine. Just be honest about it.
data.cite: Note to self after reading the forums

data.text: Summary: the signal is real but tiny and noisy. Touch is easy to detect; anything subtler needs a good amplifier and a shared ground. The project should be honest that touch drives the notes and the plant's own drift shapes the sound.

data.caption: Wiring sketch v2. Two pads on one pothos leaf, shielded cable into the amp, ESP32 sends MIDI over Wi-Fi.
First clean reading after adding a shared ground. The touch spike is easy to pick out.

data.text: Gel pads dried out within a day. Switched to small carbon pads with a clip. Readings stay stable for a week.

items.text: Map drift to filter cutoff, not pitch
Find a quieter amp for the gallery

data.text: Pitch from drift sounded like a theremin warming up. Filter from drift sounds like the room breathing. Keeping that.

data.caption: Planter cross-section. A small speaker faces down under the soil line, so sound comes from the floor.
Gallery plan. Six plants on the loop, four speakers in the corners, entry at the bottom.

data.text: Sound engine in the browser with Tone.js: each plant is one voice, a soft FM pad. Drift moves the filter; touch plays a note from a pentatonic scale so nothing clashes.

items.text: Run it for eight hours without a crash

data.caption: The room on the first evening, about 7 pm. You can hear two touches near the end.

data.text: Open studio, two evenings. People slowed down without being told. Most touched a leaf once, heard it answer, then stood and listened.
It's the first time I've waited for a plant to say something.
Next: a version for one plant on a desk, so it can live in someone's home.
